narrative:
The 2018 Washington Nationals were a team of tantalizing promise that never quite found its footing, producing one of the most maddening seasons in the franchise's recent memory. They opened with a perfect March, but April quickly turned ugly, going 11-16 as the bullpen leaked runs and opposing bats feasted on late-game situations. The low moments came early and often, from Adrian Gonzalez's grand slam off Tanner Roark to Ian Desmond's crusher off Sean Doolittle, yet Matt Adams and Howie Kendrick offered flickers of hope that kept the faithful believing a turnaround was possible.

May became the season's shining exception, a remarkable 20-7 month that stood as proof of what this roster could do when everything clicked. The offense surged, the rotation dominated, and Washington looked every bit like the playoff contender many had predicted. But the good times were fleeting. June and July combined for just 21 wins against 30 losses, and even Wilmer Difo's clutch triple and Daniel Murphy's bases-clearing single couldn't mask a club that was slowly bleeding out in the standings. Trea Turner's Independence Day grand slam offered a July highlight, but the bullpen kept surrendering the game's biggest moments.

August brought the season's most heartbreaking sequence. Ryan Madson served up David Bote's walkoff grand slam on August 12th — a -0.911 WPA catastrophe and the single most damaging play of the year — and the Cubs piled on the next day through Sammy Solís. The month somehow also produced Ryan Zimmerman's disputed but ultimately confirmed homer, an Anthony Rendon two-run shot, and a walk-off spirit that refused to die, resulting in a near-.500 August record of 14-15. By September the Nationals were playing out the string, going 15-12 in a month that showcased the emerging brilliance of Juan Soto and the departing thunder of Bryce Harper. It was a season of what-ifs: a 20-7 May surrounded by mediocrity, a bullpen that surrendered the season one grand slam at a time, and a 82-80 finish that left Washington watching October from home.

chapters.title: False Starts and Early Turbulence
chapters.description: A perfect March gives way to a rocky April as the bullpen implodes and opposing hitters deliver crushing blows, leaving Washington buried early.

chapters.title: The May Surge
chapters.description: Washington catches fire with a blistering 20-7 May, with clutch hits from Wilmer Difo and Daniel Murphy fueling the season's only dominant stretch.

chapters.title: Summer Stall
chapters.description: June and July bring a combined 21-30 record as the team struggles to sustain momentum despite bright spots like Trea Turner's Independence Day grand slam.

chapters.title: August Agony and Resilience
chapters.description: Ryan Madson's catastrophic grand slam surrender defines a brutal August stretch, though Zimmerman and Rendon provide heroic answers in a month that ends just under .500.

chapters.title: September Sendoff
chapters.description: With playoff hopes gone, Harper and the teenage sensation Juan Soto close the season with flair, going 15-12 in a bittersweet farewell to a wasted year.
